newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania vows to reform its child care system.
newsitem.headline: Romania vows to reform its child care system.

text.p: Romania is overhauling its child protection system to cope with the rising number of children abandoned in state institutions in the post-communist era, a government official said on Tuesday.

"The system needs radical reforming and nothing will be too much for us," said Cristian Tabacaru, head of the government's child protection department. "We have a duty to these 'nobody's children,' who belong to all of us."
Tabacaru was speaking at the opening here of a United Nations' Children's Fund (UNICEF) conference, focusing on the rights of institutionalised children.
The three-day event has drawn representatives from 11 East European countries, including the former Soviet Union, seeking solutions to child neglect and abuse in state institutions.
According to UNICEF data, 700,000 children live in state institutions across eastern Europe.

Romania alone has 90,000 "institutionalised" children, who are not legally abandoned by their parents, but who are in the charge of society. Their number has grown by 20 percent since the 1989 fall of communism.

Romania is trying to change the shocking image of the early post-communist years, when television pictures of scrawny and haggard children, lying in rusty cots or on cement floors in filthy orphanages were broadcast around the world.

Reformist President Emil Constantinescu, whose centrists ousted the ex-communists in last year's elections, has called for sustained efforts to end the plight of institutionalised children, which affects many of the region's post-communist societies.

"The change of political regime in 1989 has unfortunately not led to a radical change in the policy of protection of institutionalised children," said Constantinescu, visibly moved by a film on the life of children in Bucharest orphanages.
"In my room there's no other furniture except 10 cots for 17 children," said one young boy shown in the film.

Constantinescu, a father of two, said his main goal was to cut the number of institutionalised children. "First we must identify families unable to care for their children, then families willing to support them or to adopt the children."
A growing number of Romanians, hit by unemployment and plummeting living standards, are giving up their children to state institutions.
"My mother told me I must stay here until she saves enough money to build a house," said one tearful six-year-old girl. "But she never came back for me."
The government has raised child benefits to the equivalent of some $7.0 per month from $1.5 previously, and extended paid maternity leave to two years from three months.
"A child must grow up in a family. Our reform must give rights but also obligations to the families," said Tabacaru.
